newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwanese burn Japan flags in islands protest.
newsitem.headline: Taiwanese burn Japan flags in islands protest.

text.p: Hundreds of Taiwanese burned Japanese flags on Wednesday outside Japan's Taipei visa office to protest renewed Japanese claims to an East China Sea island chain that Taiwan and China both say belongs to them.
The protesters also assailed their own president's inaction in the simmering sovereignty row, and one lawmaker called on Taiwan to cooperate with Beijing and stand up to Japan.
Beijing pledged on Tuesday to take a cautious approach to calls for it to send naval forces to the uninhabited islands, saying the situation was "relatively complicated."
China is believed to be reluctant to offend Japan, whose injections of capital and technology are important to China's economy.
Wednesday's protest in Taipei came on the 65th anniversary of Japan's invasion of mainland China ahead of World War Two.

"Japan has no right to invade China again," the protesters said in a letter delivered to the Interchange Association, which acts as Tokyo's mission in Taipei in the absence of Taiwan-Japan diplomatic ties.
The protesters burned Japanese flags and beat an effigy of a Japanese in shackles, but a cordon of 50 police officers kept them from storming the downtown Taipei office.
"This is what will happen to Japan if it keeps trying to usurp the Republic of China'd sovereignty in the Diaoyus," one man shouted as protesters beat and kicked the effigy.

The director of the Japanese office, Yuki Kumamaru, accepted the letter from the private Association for the Protection of the Diaoyu Islands and pledged to pass it to Tokyo. He did not speak to the demonstrators.

The row flared in July when a Japanese rightist group built a lighthouse on one of the islands to bolster Tokyo's claim to soverignty over them. It later escalated when Japanese coast guard ships kept Taiwan vessels away from the islands, called the Diaoyus in Chinese and Senkakus in Japanese, .
Japan has not actually occupied the tiny islands.
Protests have been held in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau over Japan's activities in the potentially resource-rich islands, which Japan took as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895.
China and Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government say their claims to the Diaoyus go back centuries, but both have resisted calls to expel Japan by force.
Many of the protesters who gathered in Taipei on Wednesday also demanded Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui resign for failing to order a strong or even a military response.
"President Lee should step down," one protester shouted.
Taipei has demanded that Japan keep the rightist Japan Youth Federation at bay and dismantle the lighthouse, but has not ordered its coast guard to intervene.
Members of Taiwan's New Party, which seeks unification with China, have called on Taiwan to cooperate with Beijing and stand up to Japan.
"We cannot deprive the right of our 1.2 billion comrades to fight for our homeland," one New Party member said in a speech to the Taipei protesters.
